edition.alertText: Qatar delivers draft peace deal to Iran — 7-day confidence-building timeline, response expected by week's end; NAVCENT advises ships to avoid unnecessary Hormuz transits; Brent settles $115.32 (+1.27%) as oil rebounds; Fed holds rates at 3.75–4.00% in divided 10-2 vote; Pentagon: war cost hits $47.1B; Trump says 'anything's possible' on post-midterm strikes; WSJ: Gulf states warned to prepare for 'short, intense campaign'; Houthis strike Aden airport twice; Saudi intercepts missile toward Taif; CENTCOM rejects Iran mine claims — transit lanes 'clear'

situation: The Strait of Hormuz crisis entered day 243 with competing diplomatic and military signals leaving the conflict's near-term trajectory deeply uncertain. Qatari mediators delivered a draft peace agreement to Tehran on Sunday, setting out a seven-day timeline of daily confidence-building measures by both sides, with several countries proposed as guarantors — Iran is expected to respond by the end of the week. However, the proposal drew mixed reactions: one senior Iranian official told Reuters that Qatar had offered only 'unacceptable ideas and not an offer,' while another told The National that Iran 'welcomes any efforts aimed at negotiations, talks or collective consultation.' Separately, Iran offered a two-week pause in hostilities across the region in exchange for the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, asking Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey to persuade Washington to accept. Monday's Tehran talks involving Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin ended with a commitment to continue dialogue but no agreement on the war, Hormuz, or Iran's nuclear program. The Wall Street Journal reported that Washington warned Gulf states to prepare for a possible 'short, intense military campaign' against Iran after the November 3 midterms, while Trump said 'anything's possible' regarding post-election strikes. NAVCENT issued a new advisory on Wednesday telling vessels without essential business to 'remain well clear' of the Strait of Hormuz, citing increased traffic density and military blockade enforcement operations. October's ship attacks continued to mount — at least 30 incidents recorded this month (Washington Institute for Near East Policy), with more than 30 VLCCs damaged since the war began, about 3.5% of the global fleet (IMO). CENTCOM rejected Iranian claims that ships are hitting mines in the strait, saying all primary transit routes have been cleared and 'thousands of commercial vessels have safely used the transit lanes.'

Oil markets rebounded on Wednesday as the Ras Tanura refinery strike claim and tightening physical supplies offset diplomatic hopes. Brent crude settled at $115.32 per barrel, up $1.44 (+1.27%), recovering most of Tuesday's $2 drop. WTI settled at $102.78, up $2.88 (+2.88%), climbing back above the $100 level after briefly dipping below it the prior session. The rebound was driven by unconfirmed Houthi claims of having struck Aramco's 550,000 b/d Ras Tanura refinery, the NAVCENT advisory warning ships away from Hormuz, and a tightening Brent prompt spread still near $5. The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75–4.00% in a divided 10-2 vote, with two members preferring a quarter-point hike amid war-driven inflation — another increase in December remains in play. Gold eased to $4,035 per ounce, down 0.60% on the session, pressured by the Fed hold and a slightly firmer dollar, though ANZ noted Chinese household buying has set a floor under prices. The Pentagon disclosed that the Iran war has cost $47.1 billion as of October 16, more than 25% above July projections — roughly $29 billion for munitions replacement, $6.1 billion for lost equipment, and nearly $12 billion for operating expenses, excluding base repairs from Iranian attacks. VLCC tanker rates remained elevated at $1.2–1.4 million per day for Gulf-to-East Asia routes, with freight adding $33–41 per barrel to delivered crude. Newcastle coal held near $150 per tonne, up 40% year-to-date. OPEC+ is expected to keep December output targets unchanged at its Sunday meeting.

The Houthi-Saudi front saw continued escalation as Yemen's militia struck Aden airport twice on Wednesday — two ballistic missiles hitting the area under Saudi forces' control, halting air traffic and causing material damage and civilian injuries. The attack followed a Houthi evacuation call for the facility. Saudi air defenses intercepted a ballistic missile launched toward Taif on Tuesday night, while Houthi broadcasters claimed Saudi strikes in Yemen's Jawf province killed 14 and wounded 15 — an unverified claim. Israeli election results remained in flux with 66% of votes counted: Netanyahu's bloc was projected at 54 seats, Eisenkot's opposition at 48, and non-aligned Arab parties at a historic high of 18 — well short of the 61-seat Knesset majority, with weeks of coalition talks ahead. Netanyahu declared a 'historic, one-time opportunity' to work with Trump to 'eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all,' while Eisenkot claimed victory and vowed to replace Netanyahu's government. Treasury Secretary Bessent disclosed that Washington is tracking and freezing Iranian regime cryptocurrency assets. India's Ministry of External Affairs confirmed 22 Indian nationals have died in the conflict, including 14 seafarers. Britain issued travel warnings for 16 Middle East countries, and UAE airlines continued flight cancellations and delays, particularly on Saudi routes. Iran's Foreign Minister Araghchi warned that Israeli-instigated military action in the Gulf could have a 'devastating impact on international energy markets.'

supplyChain.name: Sulfur
supplyChain.text: Global exports down 39% YoY to 6.1M tonnes in Q2 (S&P). Sulfur prices above $1,000/tonne feeding into phosphate production costs — Egypt, Brazil, India cutting output. Mosaic idling South Fort Meade phosphate plant (Florida) for 6+ months from Dec 8 due to sulfur shortage. Morocco's OCP needs 3.7M tonnes/yr from the region. Nearly half of seaborne sulfur passed through Hormuz pre-war.

supplyChain.name: Sulfuric Acid
supplyChain.text: China banned exports Apr-Aug (700kt/yr quota replaced). SX-EW copper producers (15% of global cathode) fully exposed. Huayou cut Indonesian nickel HPAL output 50%.

supplyChain.name: Fertilizer
supplyChain.text: Fertilizer shipments through Hormuz remain near zero since early September (WTO Hormuz Trade Tracker). Urea exports from Hormuz-dependent economies fell 83% YoY in April (ITC). ~850kt urea stranded. 4 of 5 Bangladesh urea plants shut since March due to LNG shortages. FAO Food Price Index at 136 (highest since Nov 2022). UNCTAD's de la Mora warned at Doha forum (Oct 25) that farmers cutting fertilizer will hit 2027 crops; African nations face critical fuel/fertilizer shortfalls. Urea-to-corn ratio at 126 bushels/tonne vs 75 in Dec 2025 (CSIS).

supplyChain.name: LNG
supplyChain.text: Qatar LNG exports still crippled — QatarEnergy signed historic deal to buy 4M tonnes/yr US LNG from Cheniere through 2054. Putin hosted Qatar's Emir at GECF summit Oct 27 to discuss energy supplies. Dutch TTF gas near €90/MWh. Japan's trade deficit doubled to ¥2.82T ($17.8B) on higher energy costs. Kpler: Asian LNG prices to rise amid simmering geopolitical tensions.

supplyChain.name: Petrochemicals
supplyChain.text: MEG ethylene/polyethylene exports disrupted. Gulf petrochem complex cut to ~60% capacity. Methanol down 80% (ITC). Dow, LyondellBasell margins widening on supply constraint.
